newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak opposition, students vow demos will continue.
newsitem.headline: Slovak opposition, students vow demos will continue.

text.p: Slovakia's political opposition said on Friday it would continue anti-government protests despite failing to push through the sacking of two controversial ministers.

In two separate votes on Thursday evening and Friday, parliament rejected opposition motions to dismiss Culture Minister Ivan Hudec on grounds of incompetence and Interior Minister Gustav Krajci for exceeding his authority.
"The ministers remain and the disappointment over their performance also remains unchanged," Jan Budaj, opposition Democratic Union deputy chairman, told independent Radio Twist.

A strike by actors over government interference in the arts has become a focus of protest against the coalition of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar, involving students, some Roman Catholic bishops and President Michal Kovac.
The actors' strike, which has closed most Bratislava theatres and others in the country, was sparked by last year's sacking of the National Theatre director and artistic director.
Government officials say the actors and students are being manipulated by the opposition.
The affair came to a head last week when Hudec called in police to end a sit-in at his ministry by actors and supporters, including several opposition parliamentarians.
Kovac, locked in a long-running political feud with Meciar, last week added his voice to calls for Hudec to step down. The opposition claims Krajci personally ordered the police action.
"They (ministers) have nothing to lose at their posts after such an affair," Budaj said, adding that the opposition was preparing protest rallies in several towns over Slovakia.

"I wonder why they (the opposition) have been unable to invent at least one new argument...they only keep repeating the same ungrounded accusations," Hudec said on Thursday before surviving the third opposition attempt to sack him since 1994.
With several peaceful demonstrations before parliament and the Ministry of Culture already under their belts, student leaders are also vowing to continue their protests.
The unrest comes in the runnup to referendums on whether Slovaks wish to join NATO and on whether the president should be elected by direct popular vote.

Meciar's government claims Slovakia wants to be among the first new members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) but its chances seem to have slipped after U.S. and European Union criticism of the pace of democratic reform.
